doc.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Bird, Coltrane and Dinah Washington recollections
title: Reading charts and house bandleaders in the theaters
summary: Cobb says theater work required reading charts and a bandleader like Rick Henderson writing arrangements.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: In doing that, were you reading music? Or . . .
Yeah. You had to read charts and stuff like that. So you had to know all of that stuff. It was a good thing. It was a good learning process.
Did – were there instances where people didn’t have the music and you had to create it for them?
Yeah, well, they would – they had some inkling of what they needed to do, and they would tell you. We could work it out.

I know in talking with folks about the people involved at the Howard Theater, oftentimes these artists would show up. They would only have the record to go by, and you might have to create that on the spot, that day. Somebody had to be able to do that.

Yeah, somebody. It was like – usually the bandleader could probably make arrangements, write arrangements and things like that, because I know when Rick got to be the bandleader for the Howard Theater, he could do that. He could write arrangements. They could tell him what they needed. In a little time, he could produce it. He was that kind of a young, talented guy, Rick Henderson.
